notes: License-tax dispute over a bank leasing surplus office space in its own commercial office building; discusses 'right to lease as incident of ownership' but involves no dwelling/lodging occupancy.

holding_summary: The Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed a permanent injunction barring a landowner from constructing a twelve-cabin tourist camp on lots subject to a residential-use building restriction, holding that a tourist camp is a prohibited commercial use rather than a residence. The court reaffirmed that such use restrictions, unlike restraints on alienation, are valid, enforceable servitudes running with the land.

quotes.text: On September 13, 1937, F. U. Collie obtained a building permit from the city of Monroe to erect twelve tourist cabins on the property, two of the cabins to cost $500 each and the other ten cabins to cost $400 each, and pursuant to this permit entered into a contract with J. F. Heard to build the cabins.

building restrictions which restrain the use of real property for commercial purposes by prohibiting the construction of any building other than a residence or residences, and which insure a high type of construction by placing a minimum value upon any residence that may be built thereon, are not unreasonable and are not contrary to good morals, public order or express law
For the reasons assigned, the judgment appealed from is affirmed.

notes: duration_of_occupancy left unclear: the injunction issued before the tourist camp ever opened, so no actual guest-occupancy facts are in the record; who_was_letting is a planned commercial 12-cabin operation, not a householder.

holding_summary: On rehearing, the Louisiana Supreme Court reversed course and upheld Act No. 18 of 1886, which exempts hotels and boarding houses -- but not restaurants -- from the Sunday prohibition on selling wine for table use, holding the classification a permissible legislative judgment based on the nature of the hotel and boarding house business rather than unconstitutional discrimination. The restaurant proprietor's conviction was reinstated, though the charge against his clerk-employee was dismissed because the statute's penalty reaches only 'proprietors.'

quotes.text: there may still be good reason, because of the nature of the hotel and boarding house business, the investment therein, etc., for the legislature to place them in a separate and distinct class in regulating the operation of business which may be pursued on Sundays.

Act No. 18 of 1886 withstood attack, similar to that presented here, in State ex rel. Walker v. Judge, 39 La.Ann. 132, 1 So. 437. After a reconsideration, we see no reason to disturb the ruling in that case.

notes: Case concerns statutory classification of hotels/boarding houses versus restaurants under a Sunday liquor law, not a specific occupant's arrangement, so characterization/who_was_letting/duration are not applicable to a particular occupancy. On rehearing the court reversed its original opinion's discrimination holding (which had favored the restaurant) and upheld the boarding-house/hotel exemption as constitutional -- hence 'mixed' polarity.
